snip.t: A pituitary disorder is any condition that impairs the normal structure or function of the pituitary gland, leading to excess or deficiency of one or more pituitary hormones.
This is the deficiency of one or more anterior pituitary hormones.
T3 is thyroid hormone, prolactin is pituitary hormone, and ADH is produced by the hypothalamus.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: The pituitary gland releases hormones that control growth, metabolism, stress, reproduction and lactation. Clinicians must link hormone patterns to hypothalamic signals and disease states.

sections.p: The pituitary sits at the brain base and has an anterior (adenohypophysis) and posterior (neurohypophysis) lobe. The anterior lobe releases GH, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH and prolactin; the posterior releases ADH and oxytocin.
b: Anterior hormones act on peripheral endocrine organs
Feedback loops involve hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting factors

sections.p: Hypothalamic neurons secrete releasing (e.g., GHRH, TRH, CRH, GnRH) or inhibiting (e.g., somatostatin, dopamine) peptides into the portal circulation. These peptides stimulate or suppress pituitary hormone release.
b: GH → liver IGF‑1, bone growth
TSH → thyroid T3/T4 synthesis
ACTH → adrenal cortisol
LH/FSH → gonadal sex steroids & gametes
Prolactin → milk production

sections.p: Each hormone is controlled by a specific hypothalamic factor and negative feedback from its target hormone. Disruption can be primary (target organ) or secondary (pituitary/hypothalamus).
b: High cortisol suppresses CRH and ACTH
High T3/T4 suppresses TRH and TSH
High sex steroids suppress GnRH, LH, FSH

sections.p: Pituitary disease may cause excess (hyperpituitarism) or deficiency (hypopituitarism). Deficiency often presents with multiple hormone lows; excess usually reflects an adenoma secreting one hormone.
b: Pituitary adenoma → prolactinoma, GH excess, ACTH excess
Sheehan syndrome → postpartum ischemic necrosis → pan‑hypopituitarism
Infiltrative disease (TB, sarcoidosis, HIV) → hormone loss

t.a: Serum hormone panel (GH, IGF‑1, TSH, free T4, ACTH, cortisol, LH, FSH, prolactin)
t.b: Identifies which axes are deficient or excess; guides imaging

t.a: Dynamic stimulation tests (e.g., insulin tolerance, ACTH stimulation)
t.b: Distinguish pituitary vs peripheral failure; unavailable → rely on basal levels and clinical picture
Detects adenoma, infarction, infiltrative lesions; if MRI unavailable, CT can identify mass effect

sections.p: Recognising hormone patterns directs urgent treatment (e.g., adrenal crisis) and long‑term hormone replacement. Pituitary disorders can mimic common endocrine problems, so a high index of suspicion avoids misdiagnosis.
b: Low cortisol with hypotension → give IV hydrocortisone
Severe GH deficiency in children → growth hormone therapy
Prolactinoma causing infertility → dopamine agonist therapy

sections.p: Focus on feedback loops, typical presentations of hormone excess/deficiency, and the stepwise work‑up when a central cause is suspected.
b: Central hypothyroidism: low TSH + low free T4 → evaluate pituitary hormones and MRI
Hyperprolactinemia: check medication, then MRI if >200 ng/mL
ACTH‑dependent Cushing: loss of diurnal cortisol rhythm, high ACTH

whenToSeekHelp: Acute adrenal crisis (severe hypotension, vomiting, abdominal pain)
Sudden visual loss from pituitary mass compression

faq.q: Why is prolactin high in many patients on antipsychotics?
faq.a: Dopamine antagonists remove inhibition of prolactin release from the pituitary.

faq.q: Can a pituitary adenoma cause hypothyroidism?
faq.a: Yes, if it compresses normal pituitary tissue, TSH production falls leading to secondary hypothyroidism.

faq.q: What is the first test for suspected central adrenal insufficiency?
faq.a: Measure morning cortisol and ACTH; if low, confirm with a stimulation test.
